blogs.title: When Solids and Liquids Both Stick: Neurogenic Dysphagia as a Chiari Clue
blogs.description: Equal difficulty with solids and liquids plus normal laryngoscopy and endoscopy should pivot the workup away from reflux and toward neurology. We’ll outline a pragmatic pathway for persistent choking with normal scopes: targeted lower cranial nerve exam, videofluoroscopic swallow for neurogenic patterns, and early MRI of the craniocervical junction. We’ll review how lower cranial nerve involvement in Chiari I presents, why repeated GI evaluations miss it, and the diagnostic yield of reframing dysphagia as neurogenic rather than mechanical.

blogs.title: Breathing You Don’t Feel: Voluntary vs Automatic Ventilation in Chiari I
blogs.description: Profound desaturations without distress are a red flag for impaired automatic breathing with preserved voluntary control—an acquired Ondine’s curse phenotype. Using this case, we’ll connect medullary compression to lost chemosensitivity and disrupted interoceptive signaling, explaining why patients can literally forget to breathe during distraction or sleep. Practical takeaways include bedside clues, why anxiety is a tempting but wrong label, and risk mitigation around sedatives and opioids that suppress cortical drive.

blogs.title: Don’t Trust a Mild AHI: Type III Sleep Studies and Missed Central Hypoventilation
blogs.description: Type III testing uses total recording time without EEG, commonly underestimating sleep-disordered breathing severity and missing arousals and hypoventilation. We’ll show how a seemingly mild AHI can coexist with predominant central events and dangerous desaturations, and when that should trigger full polysomnography with EEG and CO2 monitoring. We’ll also cover why daytime ABGs can be normal, how to interpret a high central apnea fraction, and how to triage to the right test the first time.

blogs.title: Crowded at the Gate: Imaging Pitfalls at the Foramen Magnum
blogs.description: A “normal” head CT can conceal a crowded foramen magnum if you’re not looking for it. This post reviews what to scrutinize on legacy CTs, when sagittal MRI is indispensable, and how to think beyond the 5 mm tonsillar descent rule to a syndrome-based diagnosis. We’ll discuss cine CSF flow for decision support, common reasons Chiari is missed on initial reads, and when to request a targeted re-review from radiology.

blogs.title: Decompress or Delay? Managing Chiari I When the Problem Is Breathing
blogs.description: Posterior fossa decompression can reverse central apneas and dysphagia when brainstem compression drives symptoms, but timing is nuanced. We’ll outline indications that push toward surgery, conservative monitoring strategies, and bridging support with nocturnal noninvasive ventilation when hypoventilation is present. We’ll also address why oxygen alone can be misleading, how to set up follow-up testing, and shared decision-making that integrates symptom burden, imaging, and objective sleep data.

blogs.title: Did Trauma Cause It—or Unmask It? Navigating the Primary vs Secondary Chiari Question
blogs.description: After head or neck trauma, new occipital headaches and evolving bulbar or respiratory symptoms raise the possibility of secondary or unmasked Chiari I. We’ll summarize contemporary etiologic frameworks, why causation is hard to prove without pre-injury imaging, and how this debate should and should not influence management. Practical guidance focuses on documenting chronology, counseling patients, and keeping the therapeutic focus on current pathophysiology rather than attribution alone.
